subject: Biology
title: Cellular Nutrition and Digestion
outline: Define nutrition and distinguish autotrophic from heterotrophic modes
Describe photosynthesis, its equation, requirements, stages and experiments
Explain chemosynthesis and the roles of mineral elements in plants
Classify heterotrophic nutrition: holozoic, saprophytic, parasitic and symbiotic
Describe the human alimentary canal, digestive enzymes and absorption
Relate feeding structures and gut length to diet in different animals

modules.title: Autotrophic Nutrition: Photosynthesis and Mineral Nutrition
modules.html:
1. Modes of Nutrition

Autotrophs manufacture organic food from simple inorganic raw materials. They are photoautotrophs (using light, e.g. green plants) or chemoautotrophs (using energy from oxidising chemicals, e.g. Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter, sulphur bacteria). Heterotrophs depend on ready-made organic food.

2. Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants synthesise carbohydrate from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of light energy trapped by chlorophyll, releasing oxygen.

$$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow[\text{chlorophyll}]{\text{light energy}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$

Requirements: carbon dioxide, water, light, chlorophyll and a suitable temperature (enzymes).

3. Stages of Photosynthesis

  1. Light-dependent stage (grana of chloroplast): chlorophyll absorbs light; water is split by photolysis, \( 2H_2O \rightarrow 4H^+ + 4e^- + O_2 \); ATP and NADPH₂ are produced and oxygen is released.
  2. Light-independent stage / Calvin cycle (stroma): \( CO_2 \) is fixed and reduced using ATP and NADPH₂ to form triose sugar and eventually glucose and starch.

4. Adaptations of the Leaf

  • Broad, flat lamina – large surface area for light absorption.
  • Thin – short diffusion distance for gases.
  • Numerous stomata – gaseous exchange.
  • Palisade cells packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface.
  • Network of veins – supplies water, removes products.

5. Classic Experiments

Destarching (48 h in darkness) precedes each test; the leaf is later tested with iodine after boiling in water and in alcohol.

ExperimentVariable removedResult
Leaf partly covered with foilLightCovered part gives no blue-black colour
Variegated leafChlorophyllOnly green parts store starch
Flask with KOH in bell jarCarbon dioxideNo starch formed

6. Mineral Nutrition

ElementUseDeficiency symptom
NitrogenProteins, chlorophyll, nucleic acidsStunted growth, yellowing (chlorosis)
PhosphorusATP, nucleic acids, root growthPoor root development, purple leaves
PotassiumEnzyme activation, stomatal controlLeaf-margin scorching, weak stems
MagnesiumCentral atom of chlorophyllChlorosis between veins
IronChlorophyll synthesis, cytochromesChlorosis of young leaves
CalciumMiddle lamella of cell wallDeath of growing points

examples.q: Why is a leaf boiled in alcohol before the iodine test?
examples.a: Boiling in water first kills the cells and makes the leaf permeable; boiling in alcohol removes the chlorophyll so that the green colour does not mask the blue-black colour produced when iodine reacts with any starch present. The brittle leaf is then softened in warm water before adding iodine.

examples.q: State the balanced equation for photosynthesis and identify what is oxidised and what is reduced.
examples.a: $$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$ Water is oxidised (it loses hydrogen/electrons during photolysis, releasing \(O_2\)) while carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrate.

modules.title: Heterotrophic Nutrition and the Human Digestive System
modules.html:
1. Types of Heterotrophic Nutrition

  • Holozoic – solid food is ingested, digested, absorbed, assimilated and egested (most animals). Sub-types: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore.
  • Saprophytic – feeding on dead organic matter by extracellular digestion (Rhizopus, mushrooms, many bacteria).
  • Parasitic – living in or on a host, causing harm (tapeworm, Plasmodium, mistletoe).
  • Symbiotic / mutualistic – both partners benefit (Rhizobium in legume root nodules; lichens = alga + fungus; cellulose-digesting bacteria in the rumen).

2. Processes of Holozoic Nutrition

Ingestion → digestion (mechanical and chemical) → absorption → assimilation → egestion.

3. The Human Alimentary Canal

RegionSecretionEnzymeSubstrate → Product
MouthSaliva (pH 7)Salivary amylase (ptyalin)Starch → maltose
StomachGastric juice + HCl (pH 2)Pepsin; rennin in infantsProtein → peptides; caseinogen → casein
DuodenumPancreatic juice + bileAmylase, trypsin, lipaseStarch → maltose; protein → peptides; fat → fatty acids + glycerol
IleumIntestinal juice (succus entericus)Maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidase, lipaseDisaccharides → monosaccharides; peptides → amino acids

Bile from the liver contains no enzyme; bile salts emulsify fats, increasing surface area for lipase, and bile neutralises the acidic chyme.

4. Absorption and Assimilation

Absorption occurs mainly in the ileum, whose villi are adapted by: a very large surface area, one-cell-thick epithelium, dense capillary network for amino acids and glucose, a lacteal for fatty acids and glycerol, and many mitochondria for active transport. Absorbed food goes via the hepatic portal vein to the liver, where glucose may be stored as glycogen and excess amino acids are deaminated to urea.

5. Dentition and Diet

Herbivores have sharp incisors, a diastema and ridged molars for grinding, plus a long gut and caecum harbouring cellulose-digesting bacteria. Carnivores have pointed canines and carnassial teeth for shearing flesh and a comparatively short gut.

examples.q: Why is the ileum longer and more folded than any other part of the gut?
examples.a: It is the main site of absorption. Length, circular folds, villi and microvilli together create an enormous surface area — several hundred square metres in an adult — so digested nutrients can be absorbed rapidly and completely by diffusion and active transport.

examples.q: Explain the role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
examples.a: HCl (i) provides the acidic pH of about 2 required for pepsin activity, (ii) converts inactive pepsinogen to active pepsin, (iii) kills most bacteria swallowed with food and (iv) stops the action of salivary amylase.

modules.title: Balanced Diet, Food Tests and Deficiency Diseases
modules.html:
1. Classes of Food

Carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats and oils (energy store, insulation), vitamins and mineral salts (protective), water and roughage.

Food substanceTestPositive result
StarchIodine solutionBlue-black colour
Reducing sugarBenedict’s solution, boilBrick-red precipitate
ProteinBiuret (NaOH + CuSO₄)Purple/violet colour
Fat/oilFilter paper or Sudan IIITranslucent spot / red-stained layer

2. Vitamins and Deficiency Diseases

Vitamin/mineralSourceDeficiency
A (retinol)Carrot, palm oil, liverNight blindness, xerophthalmia
B₁ (thiamine)Whole grains, beansBeri-beri
C (ascorbic acid)Citrus, guavaScurvy
D (calciferol)Sunlight, fish oilRickets, osteomalacia
CalciumMilk, fish bonesWeak bones, poor clotting
IronLiver, leafy vegetablesAnaemia
IodineSea food, iodised saltGoitre, cretinism

3. Protein-Energy Malnutrition

Kwashiorkor results from protein deficiency with adequate carbohydrate: oedema, pot-belly, sparse discoloured hair, retarded growth. Marasmus results from overall energy and protein deficiency: extreme wasting, 'old man' face. Both are treated with a balanced, protein-rich diet.

4. Energy Value of Food

Energy from food is measured in joules or kilocalories using a bomb calorimeter, where \( Q = mc\Delta\theta \), with \(m\) the mass of water, \(c = 4.2\,\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \( \Delta\theta \) the temperature rise.

examples.q: 1 g of groundnut raised the temperature of 20 g of water by 25 °C. Calculate the energy released.
A child has oedema, a pot belly and pale hair but eats plenty of yam. Diagnose and prescribe.
examples.a: The child suffers from kwashiorkor, a protein deficiency; the diet is rich in carbohydrate but poor in protein. Treatment is a gradual increase of first-class protein — milk, eggs, fish, beans, soya — together with vitamins and minerals.

quiz.q: The raw materials for photosynthesis are
quiz.solution: CO₂ and H₂O are converted into carbohydrate with oxygen as by-product.

quiz.q: The light-dependent stage of photosynthesis occurs in the
quiz.solution: Chlorophyll is located on the thylakoid membranes of the grana where light is absorbed.

quiz.q: Photolysis of water during photosynthesis produces
quiz.solution: Water is split into H⁺, electrons and molecular oxygen.

quiz.q: The element that forms the central atom of a chlorophyll molecule is
quiz.solution: Magnesium is at the centre of the porphyrin ring of chlorophyll; its deficiency causes chlorosis.

quiz.q: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are examples of
quiz.solution: They obtain energy by oxidising ammonia and nitrite respectively, not from light.

quiz.q: A leaf is boiled in alcohol during the starch test in order to
quiz.solution: Decolourising the leaf allows the blue-black iodine colour to be seen.

quiz.q: Which of the following organisms feeds saprophytically?
quiz.solution: Rhizopus secretes enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbs the soluble products.

quiz.q: The association between Rhizobium and leguminous roots is an example of
quiz.solution: The bacterium fixes nitrogen for the plant and receives carbohydrate and shelter in return.

quiz.q: Pepsin works best at a pH of about
quiz.solution: Gastric HCl provides a strongly acidic medium of about pH 2 for pepsin.

quiz.q: Bile aids digestion of fats by
quiz.solution: Bile salts lower surface tension, breaking fat into tiny droplets and enlarging the surface for lipase.

quiz.q: The end products of protein digestion are
quiz.solution: Peptidases complete the breakdown of peptides into amino acids in the ileum.

quiz.q: Fatty acids and glycerol absorbed in the ileum enter the
quiz.solution: They are absorbed into the lacteal of the villus and enter the lymphatic system.

quiz.q: Which food substance gives a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's solution on boiling?
quiz.solution: Reducing sugars such as glucose reduce copper(II) to red copper(I) oxide.

quiz.q: Deficiency of vitamin C in the diet causes
quiz.solution: Ascorbic acid deficiency weakens connective tissue, causing bleeding gums and scurvy.

quiz.q: A pot-bellied child with oedema and discoloured hair most likely suffers from
quiz.solution: These are the classical signs of protein deficiency (kwashiorkor).

quiz.q: The main function of roughage in the diet is to
quiz.solution: Indigestible cellulose adds bulk to the food, encouraging peristaltic movement of the gut.
